text:
I decoded and measured the whole chunk, and there
  are four levels of redundancy stacked here, escalating to
  one that should make you laugh:

  Level 1 — within-row RLE. Already done (that's the
  [count, value] runs).

  Level 2 — the [2,3] is part of a bigger motif. The road
  cross-section (3,13)(18)(3,12) repeats 190 times; the
  full sidewalk-bracketed profile
  (4,3)(3,13)(18)(3,12)(41,3) repeats 74 times. So [2,3]
  isn't the pattern — it's the shoulder of one recurring
  road-profile token that's getting re-spelled ~190×.

  Level 3 — whole rows repeat. 120 rows decode to only 34 
  unique rows. 77 of 119 consecutive rows are byte-for-byte
  identical. The per-row RLE re-spells every row even when
  it's identical to the one above it — because the roads
  run vertically, and 1D row-RLE is blind to vertical
  coherence. (This is the 2D-vs-1D thing: you're RLE-ing
  one axis of a two-axis-coherent grid.)

  Level 4 — and here's the "even more than that": you're 
  storing the roads twice. Look at what's in the same file:
  - roads: 17 segments, 2.6KB, every one an axis-aligned 
  straight line ((30,5)→(30,57), etc.), and all 17 share 
  the exact same profile {1 lane each way, sidewalks, 
  50kph}.
  - tiles: 11.6KB — 82% of the file — which is the 
  rasterization of those exact roads stamped onto a
  background (value 3 is 54.5% of the grid = the base
  ground; the road cells are ~20%).
  
  That 190×-repeated cross-section motif IS that one shared
  profile, stamped along the polylines. The tiles are the
  baked raster of the roads vector that's sitting right 
  next to them in the same JSON. You have the recipe
  (roads, 18% of the file) and its baked result (tiles,
  82%) stored side by side.

  So the reason it "still isn't doing the right thing": the
  extractor rasterizes the vector roads into the tile grid
  and then stores both. That's
  storing-the-result-when-the-recipe-is-right-there — the
  exact move the whole architecture says don't. It's the
  raster-vs-vector map-tile thing from before, in
  miniature: tiles = raster (baked, huge), roads = vector
  (recipe, tiny).

  The fix, escalating:

  - Mechanical (stay in tile format): dedup rows → 34
  unique + 120 indices (~3.5× on the row data), and
  tokenize that road cross-section motif. This compresses
  the symptom.
  - The actual fix (store recipe, not result): don't 
  rasterize roads into tiles at bake. Store: (a) the base 
  terrain only — the non-road background, which is ~54% one
  value and RLEs to almost nothing; (b) the roads vector —
  already there, and since all 17 share one profile, dedup
  it to a single profile entry so each road is just
  (start, end, profileRef) ≈ a few hundred bytes total; (c)
  a "rasterize at load" flag. The loader stamps profile →
  cross-section along each polyline onto the base. The
  cross-section is a pure function of the profile; the
  stamp is a pure function of the line — fully
  deterministic, fully derivable. 11.6KB of tiles → ~2–3KB
  of base + a few hundred bytes of roads.

  The tell is poetic: the redundant motif you spotted is
  literally the shape of the one road profile that's 
  already stored as data three feet away in the same file.
  The extractor is doing the bake the loader should be
  doing at load.
